{ "item": { "id": "062cc815-2b65-45b1-b36c-6ea67dfd1a0c", "content_type": "generic", "workflow_state": "public", "page_title": "Handling errors & retries", "short_description": "How Godzilla retries failed events, when they're dead-lettered, and how to replay them.", "body": "

Handling errors & retries

Every event that fails a transform or a destination write is retried automatically. This guide covers how that works and what to do when retries run out.

Automatic retries

Failed events retry with exponential backoff — 1s, 2s, 4s, up to a per-pipeline configurable ceiling. Most transient failures (a destination hiccup, a rate-limited third party) resolve within the first few attempts.

{{ds:component/code-block|filename=pipeline-retry-config.json|language=json|code={ "retry_policy": { "max_attempts": 5, "backoff": "exponential", "initial_delay_ms": 1000 } }}}

Dead-lettering

An event that exhausts its retries is moved to that pipeline's dead-letter queue rather than dropped silently.

{{ds:component/alert|variant=danger|title=Dead-lettered events don't retry themselves|body_html=

Once in the dead-letter queue, an event stays there until you replay it or explicitly discard it — it will not retry again on its own.

}}

Replaying events

Use the Events endpoint's replay action to re-run a specific dead-lettered event once the underlying issue is fixed.

{{ds:component/code-block|filename=replay.sh|language=bash|code=curl -X POST https://api.godzilladocs.dev/v2/events/evt_8f2c1a90/replay \ -H "Authorization: Bearer $GODZILLA_API_KEY"}}

Watching for failures

Subscribe to pipeline.failed via Webhooks so you find out about dead-lettered events before a customer does. See also Monitoring & alerts.

{{ds:component/docs-pagination|prev_href={{cms:item/3448ffab-598c-46e7-bda6-e7cdc4a1e7c6}}|prev_label=Connecting a data source|next_href={{cms:item/dc9f1302-e173-4034-9581-d06efea7d090}}|next_label=Scheduling & triggers}}", "version_token": "28b32bfd-c5c0-4f68-abd2-948e70c8a38d", "created_at": "2026-08-20T14:12:40.183Z", "updated_at": "2026-08-20T15:07:12.082Z", "placement_id": "0b6c15be-6394-4b2e-80ca-660125cbee7b", "folder_id": "c3e0ba4a-a491-4265-9848-556d298e6b6b", "file_name": "handling-errors-and-retries" } }

content.text: Now I'll create the new guide page:

input.short_description: Reshape, filter, and enrich events as they pass through a pipeline using transforms.
input.body:
Transforming events in flight

Once you've connected a source and a destination, the next step is to shape and enrich your data. This guide covers how to use transforms to reshape fields, filter events, and enrich your data as it flows through your pipeline.

What are transforms?

A transform is a function that runs on every event as it passes through your pipeline, after it's read from the source but before it reaches the destination. Transforms can:

  • Reshape fields (rename, extract, flatten, or nest data)
  • Filter events (drop events that don't meet criteria)
  • Enrich events (add new fields, lookup data, compute derived values)
  • Validate events (ensure required fields and data types)

Adding a transform to your pipeline

Transforms are added as a stage between your source and destination connectors. When you create or edit a pipeline, you can insert one or more transforms into the event flow.

{{ds:component/code-block|filename=pipeline-with-transform.json|language=json|code={\n \"name\": \"customer-sync\",\n \"source\": {\n \"connector_id\": \"postgres-prod\",\n \"table\": \"customers\"\n },\n \"transforms\": [\n {\n \"type\": \"reshape\",\n \"mappings\": {\n \"customer_id\": \"id\",\n \"email_address\": \"email\"\n }\n }\n ],\n \"destination\": {\n \"connector_id\": \"webhook-crm\"\n }\n}}}

Reshaping fields

Reshape transforms let you rename, extract, or reorganize fields in your event. This is useful when your source and destination use different field names or structures.

{{ds:component/code-block|filename=reshape-example.json|language=json|code={\n \"type\": \"reshape\",\n \"mappings\": {\n \"customer_id\": \"id\",\n \"order_amount\": \"total_price\",\n \"created_at\": \"timestamp\"\n }\n}}}

For nested data, use dot notation to extract or create nested fields:

{{ds:component/code-block|filename=nested-reshape.json|language=json|code={\n \"type\": \"reshape\",\n \"mappings\": {\n \"user.first_name\": \"first_name\",\n \"user.last_name\": \"last_name\",\n \"billing_address.zip\": \"zip_code\"\n }\n}}}

Filtering events

Filter transforms drop events that don't match a condition, so only relevant data reaches your destination.

{{ds:component/alert|variant=info|title=Filtered events are not retried|body_html=

When an event is filtered out, it's considered successfully processed and won't appear in your dead-letter queue.

}} {{ds:component/code-block|filename=filter-example.json|language=json|code={\n \"type\": \"filter\",\n \"condition\": \"event.order_amount > 100\"\n}}}

Enriching events

Enrichment transforms add new fields to your events, pulling data from external sources, computing derived values, or adding context.

{{ds:component/code-block|filename=enrichment-example.json|language=json|code={\n \"type\": \"enrich\",\n \"lookups\": [\n {\n \"field\": \"user_id\",\n \"source\": \"user-database\",\n \"target_field\": \"user_profile\"\n }\n ],\n \"computed_fields\": {\n \"total_vat\": \"event.order_amount * 0.2\",\n \"region\": \"event.country.substring(0, 2)\"\n }\n}}}

Chaining transforms

Multiple transforms execute in order: the output of one becomes the input to the next. This lets you build complex logic step by step.

{{ds:component/code-block|filename=chained-transforms.json|language=json|code={\n \"transforms\": [\n { \"type\": \"filter\", \"condition\": \"event.status !== 'cancelled'\" },\n { \"type\": \"reshape\", \"mappings\": { \"order_id\": \"id\" } },\n { \"type\": \"enrich\", \"computed_fields\": { \"processed_at\": \"new Date().toISOString()\" } }\n ]\n}}}

Testing transforms

Before deploying a transform to production, use the pipeline preview feature to run a sample event through your transforms and see the output. This helps catch logic errors early.

Performance considerations

Each transform adds latency to your event processing. For high-throughput pipelines, consider:

  • Combining multiple field mappings into a single reshape transform
  • Placing filter transforms early to reduce data moving through subsequent transforms
  • Using batch enrichment lookups when possible instead of per-event lookups

Next steps

With transforms reshaping and enriching your data, follow Handling errors & retries to learn how to manage failures in your pipeline.

input.body:
Connecting a data source

This guide covers choosing and configuring a source connector — the first step of any new pipeline.

Choosing a connector type

You haveUse
A relational database you can grant replication access toPostgres
Files landing in object storageAmazon S3
An existing event streamKafka
A third party that can push to a URL you controlWebhook

Authenticating

Each connector type has its own credential shape — see the Connectors endpoint for the full parameter list per type.

{{ds:component/alert|variant=warning|title=Least-privilege credentials|body_html=

Grant the connector only the access it needs — read-only replication for Postgres sources, a scoped IAM role for S3, never a superuser or admin credential.

}}

Verifying the connection

A newly created connector reports health: degraded until its first successful read or write, then flips to healthy. If it goes straight to down, double check credentials before opening a support ticket.

Next steps

With a source connected, follow Transforming events in flight to reshape and enrich your data as it flows through the pipeline.

{{ds:component/docs-pagination|prev_href={{cms:item/2df76640-838b-4256-956e-d8a19a602241}}|prev_label=Building your first pipeline|next_href={{cms:item/ffecea27-f0aa-4b8d-95af-7b01b2d5dfc9}}|next_label=Transforming events in flight}}

Handling errors & retries

Every event that fails a transform or a destination write is retried automatically. This guide covers how that works and what to do when retries run out.

Automatic retries

Failed events retry with exponential backoff — 1s, 2s, 4s, up to a per-pipeline configurable ceiling. Most transient failures (a destination hiccup, a rate-limited third party) resolve within the first few attempts.

{{ds:component/code-block|filename=pipeline-retry-config.json|language=json|code={\n \"retry_policy\": {\n \"max_attempts\": 5,\n \"backoff\": \"exponential\",\n \"initial_delay_ms\": 1000\n }\n}}}

Dead-lettering

An event that exhausts its retries is moved to that pipeline's dead-letter queue rather than dropped silently.

{{ds:component/alert|variant=danger|title=Dead-lettered events don't retry themselves|body_html=

Once in the dead-letter queue, an event stays there until you replay it or explicitly discard it — it will not retry again on its own.

}}

Replaying events

Use the Events endpoint's replay action to re-run a specific dead-lettered event once the underlying issue is fixed.

{{ds:component/code-block|filename=replay.sh|language=bash|code=curl -X POST https://api.godzilladocs.dev/v2/events/evt_8f2c1a90/replay \\\n -H \"Authorization: Bearer $GODZILLA_API_KEY\"}}

Watching for failures

Subscribe to pipeline.failed via Webhooks so you find out about dead-lettered events before a customer does. See also Monitoring & alerts.

{{ds:component/docs-pagination|prev_href={{cms:item/ffecea27-f0aa-4b8d-95af-7b01b2d5dfc9}}|prev_label=Transforming events in flight|next_href={{cms:item/dc9f1302-e173-4034-9581-d06efea7d090}}|next_label=Scheduling & triggers}}
